full_judgment:
Ruhul Islam J.- This appeal by special leave which arises out of a pre-emption proceeding under section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act, 1949. The respondents filed application under section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act, 1949 for pre-emption of the auction sale on 24-10-1973 in Certificate Case No 408 of 1967-1968 held by the Certificate Officer, Chittagong, for arrear rent dues from H E Percival, the recorded tenant, transferring land of P.S. Plot No. 108 of P.S. Khatian No. 14. The respondents claimed to be co-sharers of the Certificate Debtor by purchase of 1 kani 10 gondas of land of plot Nos. 107 and 87 appertaining to said Khatian No. 14, from H.E. Percival by registered kabala dated 29-12-1965 and their names were duly mutated in Khatian No. 14, which has been described in Schedule No. 2, which is part of Schedule 1 containing P.S. Khatians Nos. 14, 18, 20 and 24 owned by H.E. Percival in Mouza Kashim Bazar, P.S. Kotwali Chittagong, Their further case is that in the Oerti6cate Sale it was wrongly shown that P.S. Plot No. 108 appertained to P.S. Khatian No. 18 created after amalgamation and consolidation of the holdings held by H.E. Percival, because, such ambulation was done without giving any notice to the co-sharers. The pre-emption case was contested by the pre-emptee contending inter alia that the pre-emptors though were co sharers of the P.S. Khatian No. 14, but they ceased to be co-sharers after the lands in different plots in Kbatian Nos. 14, 18, 20 and 24 in Mouza Kashim Bazar still owned and possessed by H.E. Percival were amalgamated and consolidated in one Khatian, namely Khatian No. 18 and the auction sale was held on the basis of the new Khatian No. 18, wherein they were not co-sharers of the Certificate Debtor. 

 2. The pre-emption case was dismissed by the learned Subordinate Judge and on appeal the learned District Judge. Chittagong allowed the pre-emption case in part and remanded the case to the trial Court for assessment of the cost of improvement in the case land. The appellant unsuccessfully moved the High Court Division in revision and thereafter obtained leave from this Court. Leave was granted to examine the question whether after creation of a new tenancy by amalgamation and consolidation of holdings the respondent pre-emptors could rightly claim to be co-sharers of the recorded tenant H.E. Percival. Leave was also granted to consider the question whether a person claiming to be co-sharer in the holding, and not in the land transferred, could validly, maintain an application for pre- emption under section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act, 1949. 

 4. Mr. Hamidul Huq Chowdbury, the learned Counsel appearing for the appellant submitted that amalgamation and consolidation of holdings having been made by the Revenue Officer in due course of his official duties, it should be presumed that it was validly done and in accordance with law, besides it is not correct to say that a new tenancy in P.S Khatian No. 18 in the name of H.E. Percival as the sole owner was made in the absence of any written application by the recorded tenant H.E. Percival in this regard; and the order was made without giving any notice to the co-sharers of H.E, Percival. With reference to different documents on record the learned Counsel submitted that the record would show that the amalgamation proceeding was initiated at the instance of H. E. Percival. When Certificate Case No. 408/67-68 and six other Certificate Cases were started against H.E. Percival by the Certificate Officer Chittagong for realization or arrear rents, on 12-3-69, the certificate debtor filed an application under section 9 of the Public Demands Recovery Act. in the aforesaid 7 Certificate Cases denying his liability for the huge arrear revenue dues on the grounds, inter alia that the lands of some of the khatians had been acquired by the Government and some of the lands bad been transferred by him to different persons; and praying for permission to pay the proportionate amount of the rent dues for him existing land in different khatians. On this application an order was passed by the Certificate Officer on 21-6-1973 directing the Tahsilder concerned for filing revised certificate on fresh assessment of correct rental dues, after amalgamation and consolidation of the lands in deferent khatians still in the possessions of H.E. Percival. The learned Counsel submitted that a regular case under Chapter XV of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act was started by the Revenue Officer concerned and as a result new khatian No. 18 solely in the name of H.E. Percival was created, and on the basis of this khatian revised certificate was filed. The learned Counsel further submitted that auction was held on the basis of this amalgamated newly created khatian No. 18 wherein the respondents not being co- sharer are not entitled to pre-empt the certificate sale 

 5. On perusal of the material on record it appears that admittedly the land of khatian No. 18 was sold in auction for arrears of rent and the pre-emptors were not co- sharers in the said khatian. H.E. Percival was a recorded tenant in respect of khatian Nos. 14, 18, 20 and 24, and for recovery of a huge arrear of rent in respect of those khatians Certificate Case Nos. 408, 109, 411, 412, 413 and 414 of 1967-68 were started. H.E. Percival filed an application under section 9 of Public Demands Recovery Act, 1913 on 12-3-69 stating inter alia that he was not liable for the entire arrear rent dues, because some of the lands had been acquired by the Government and some of the lands had been transferred by him to different persons. He stated therein that he was prepared to pay the proportionate rent for the lands still in his possession. This application was duly signed by H.E. Percival. On this application, it appears from the order sheet that the relevant Revenue authority took certain actions on the direction of the Circle Officer (Revenue) and a proposal for consolidation and amalgamation of several holdings of H.E. Percival was submitted, and on the basis of this recommendation for amalgamation and consolidation the relevant Revenue Officer passed the order. From the Circular of the Board of Revenue dated 26-6-69 it appears that the district authorities were instructed to the effect that the work of amalgamation of holdings should be started in all the circles in the month of July and complete by the end of October, 1969. Mr. Hamidul Huq Chowdhury, rightly pointed out with reference to the Circular that the amalgamation of the lands belonging to H E. Percival was not a solitary case, because, the process of amalgamation and consolidation had already been started in the district There is no doubt the action was taken at the instance of H.E. Percival, and it was taken up in this background Chapter XV of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act provides for amalgamation, sub-division and consolidation of holdings. Section 116 provides that where various parcels of land are held by One tenant within one village, and such parcels of land or some of them are the subject of separate tenancies, such parcels of land shall under the orders of the Revenue- officer, be amalgamated into one tenancy. Section 117 provides the at notwithstanding anything contained elsewhere in this part, the Revenue-officer may.- 

 (c)for the purpose of sub-division of a joint tenancy for distribution of rent thereof, on an application made to him by one or more co- sharer tenants..................’' 

 Chapter XVII of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act provides for maintenance and revision of the record- of fights. Section 143 of the Act provides that the Collector shall maintain up-to-date, in the prescribed manner, the record-of rights prepared or revised under Part IV or under this Chapter by correcting clerical mistakes and by incorporating therein the changes on account of- 

 6. With reference to section 117 of the Act Khondkarm Mahbubuddin Ahmed submitted that the entire proceedings and the purported amalgamation and consolidation of holdings as claimed by the appellant being not in accordance with Jaw, was illegal, and as such the new khatian 18 having no legal basis, it should be presumed that the khatians 14, 18, 20 and 24 continued to be the existing khatians and khatian 14 to which Plot No. 108 appertained, the respondents continued to be co-sharers of H.E. Percival in the said, holding, and it is not correct to say that H.E. Percival was the sole owner of Plot No. 108 without any co-sharer, He also argued that the purported amalgamation and consolidation of holdings under section 116 of the Act was done without giving any notice to the co-sharers. In the absence of any notice upon the co-sharers the alleged amalgamation and consolidation of holding is not tenable in law. Mr. Hamidul Huq Chowdhury, however submitted by pointing out from the record that the noting in the order sheet of Miscellaneous Case No. 89 of 1972-73 (under Chapter XV of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act) sufficiently showed that amalgamation and consolidation of holdings of HE. Percival was made after the service of notice on all the parties concerned as per provisions of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. 

 8. In view of the circumstances as noted above, it would not be correct to say that the proceeding for amalgamation and consolidation of holdings under sections 116 and 117 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act was initiated suo motu without having any basis. In the auction sale P.S. Plot No. 108 as appearing appertained to new P.S. Khatian No. 18 was sold. It is admitted that plot No. 108 previously appertained to khatian No. 14, and in its 16 annas belonged to H.E. Percival. So separation of plot No.108 from khatian No. 14 and its amalgamation in khatian No. 18, could not prejudice the pre-emptors who claimed to be a co- sharer in khatian No. 14 on the basis of their purchase from H.E. Percival. Apart from that there is a presumption under the law that all official acts are presumed to have been rightly and regularly done. 

 9. Chapter XV of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act deals with "Amalgamation Sub-division and Consolidation of holdings." Section 116 provides for amalgamation of holding of a tenant in the same village. This section requires that where various parcels of land are held by one tenant within one village and such parcels of land or some of them are the subject of separate tenancies such parcels of land shall under the orders of the Revenue-officer, be amalgamated into one tenancy. This section however provides that if the tenant concerned has any objection thereto which appears to such officer to be reasonable and sufficient no such amalgamation shall be ordered by the Revenue-officer. Section 116 read with section 117(1) (a) provides that amalgamation and consolidation can be taken by the Revenue-officer, either on his own motion or on an application made to him, in that behalf Section 17(1)(c) contains the provision for sub-division of a joint tenancy for distribution of rent thereof subject to the conditions indicated therein. On examining sections 116 and 117 Hind that the learned Judge of the High Court Division is completely in error in taking the view that it is a case of sub-division of a joint tenancy as provided under section 117(1)(c) for which an application was required to be filed; and in the absence of an application by the parties the Revenue officer had no authority of his own motion to sub-divide a joint tenancy. He was however conscious that "Amalgamation and consolidation as have been referred in the section may begin for the purpose of collection of revenue and for that purpose the Revenue-officer may on his own motion exercise jurisdiction." The relevant finding of the learned' Judge is quoted below: 

 "So I am of the view that for the purpose of sub-division of a joint tenancy an application must be filed by the tenant concerned. In the instant case the typed copy of the application dated 12.3.69 in the certificate case before the Certificate Officer at Chittagong under section 9 of the P.D.R. Act for dismissing the certificate cases could not be suo motu brought in the Miscellaneous case No. 89/72-73 by the Revenue Officer" 

 10. Khondkar	Mahbubuddin	Ahmed only faintly argued that as a matter of fact this was a case of sub-division of a joint tenancy. He however failed to give sufficient reasons in support of this view. Prior to amalgamation Khatian No. 14 contained plot Nos. 108, 107, 87 and 124; Khatian No. 20 contained Plot No. 116; and Kbatian No. 24 contained plots 117 and 121. By the process of amalgamation and consolidation Plot 108 of Khatian 14, plot 119 of khatian 18, plot 16 of khatian 20 and plots 117 and 121 of khatian 24 were amalgamated and consolidated into one khatian, that is khatian 18. This sufficiently shows that it was a case of amalgamation and consolidation as contemplated under section 116 read with section 117(1)(a) and not a case of sub-division of a tenancy recorded in kbatian 14, as provided in section 1l7(1)(c). The order of the Certificate officer who was also the Revenue Officer, shows that the action for amalgamation and consolidation was taken at the instance of the tenant when it was considered necessary for the purpose of collection of revenue. Plot 108 solely owned and possessed by H. E. Percival was amalgamated with Plot No. 119 of khatian 18 plot No. 116 of Khatian No. 20 and plot Nos. 117 and 121 of khatian 24 and thereby new khatian 18 was brought into being and a new jama was fixed for the amalgamated and consolidated khatian. Endorsement on khatian 14 filed by the respondents itself shows that separation of plot No. 108 from that khatian and its amalgamation to khatian 18 was noted on it. Payment of rent at the old rate even after the amalgamation and consolidation as claimed by the respondents cannot set at naught the process and the order of amalgamation and consolidation which was duly made and acted upon. The learned Subordinate Judge took the correct view on this question saying:- 

 “As there was no short payment it was accepted when the petitioners paid rent at the old rate. This payment of rent at the previous rate itself does not show that the amalgamation and separation of tenancy was not given effect to." 

 11. There is another point to be discussed which is that the learned District Judge as wen as the learned Judge of the High Court Division took the view that the so called amalgamation and consolidation of holdings suo motu and that too after death of H.E. Percival cannot be said to have any legal sanction and must be treated as a void one and need not be avoided. Mr. Hamidul Huq Chowdhury In support of his submissions that the order of amalgamation and consolidation was made in accordance with law, further submitted that when such an order has been passed by the competent authority and in accordance with law, its validity cannot be challenged in the pre-emption proceeding. In support of this proposition he relied upon a decision of this Court in the case of Md. Jabed Ali Vs. Pakhal Chandra Mondal, 33 DLR (AD) 309. This is a case of separation of jam a under section 117(1) (c) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act and not a case of amalgamation and consolidation, but the principle laid down therein provides the necessary guidance. In that case it has been held as follows:- 

 14. The land under pre-emption is plot No. 108 of Khatian No. 14 which belonged to one Percival. Khatian No. 14 consisted of three plots, Nos. 87, 107 and 108 and this Khatian, it is needless to say, constituted a non-agricultural holding under Percival. Respondent, pre-emptor purchased Plots Nos. 87 and 107 by a registered kabala dated 29 December 1965 and thereby became a co-sharer in the holding and in due course his name was mutated as Percival's co-sharer under a joint Jarna of Rs.4 and annas 7. Percival also held many other parcels of land such as in Khatians Nos. 18, 20 and 24, but the Respondent is not interested in those lands as he is not a co-sharer there. A Certificate Case being C.C. No. 408 of 1967-68 along with other such cases was filed against Percival for recovery of money due asarrear of rent under the Public Demands Recovery Act, 1913 and this case was pending when he die in August, 1971. Two years five months after his death that is, on 24 December 1973, the appellant-pre-emptee, a stranger, auction purchased Plot No 108 along with other lands of Percival in connection with that Certificate Case. Respondent filed the pre-emption case on 15 April 1976, under section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act alleging that he had come to know of the sale for the first time on 3 January 1976. He further alleged in his application that by an inquiry be had ascertained that, for the purpose of avoiding pre-emption, the pre-emptee had, by collusion with the Revenue Officer, got a Mutation case, being Miscellaneous Case No. 89 of 1972-73, started and thereby made a show of separation of Plot No. 108 from the joint tenancy under Khatian No. 14 and amalgamation of the separted hare with the other lands of late Percival, which were shown constipated as a new tenancy under Khatian N.18. Separation of this plot from the original holding having been made in total disregard of mandatory provisions of section 117(c) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, the pre-emptor alleged, the separation is void and not binding upon him and that he continued to be a co-sharer of the holding in Khatian No. 14. 

 15. The application for pre-emption was resisted on grounds of limitation and maintainability, particularly the latter. It was contended that "the separation and amalgamation" was effected by the Revenue Officer in accordance with law and that the Revenue Officer's order could not be challenged in a collateral proceeding like the pre-emption case. The trial Court accepted both the grounds and refused pre-emption holding the pre-emptor ceased to be a co. sharer in the holding since 24 April 1973 when plot No. 108 of Percival was validly separated from the original holding. But on appeal the learned District Judge reversed the findings on both the points and allowed the pre-eruption subject to payment of compensation for improvement of the land the amount of which was to be determined on remand after arriving at the findings that the Revenue Officer's order for separation of Percival's share was void in that the said order was passed by the Revenue Officer "on his own motion's and not upon any application from a co-sharer and that no notice of the 'Separation' was served upon the other co-sharer and further that the order was also acted upon as rent of the joint tenancy continued to be paid at the old rate. A learned Single Judge of the High Court Division did not find anything to interfere with the District Judge's order in revision. 

 16. Leave was granted on both the grounds, limitation and maintainability, but the ground as to the limitation was not pressed. Mr. Hamidul Huq Chowdhury, learned Counsel for the appellants directed his arguments on the question of maintainability of the application for pre-emption contending that the respondent ceased to be a co-sharer in the holding since the separation of Percival's share and creation of a new tenancy comprising the separated portion and other lands of Percival. Mr. Chowdhury next contends that when the Record of the Revenue Officer prima facie shows the separation and amalgamation according to law, his order cannot be challenged in a collateral proceeding like the instant one. Yes, if the original holding under Khatian No.14 were subdivided and plot No. 108 were separated therefrom according to law, then the pre-emptor got no case, as on sub-division of an original holding the former co-sharers cease to remain co-sharers with right to pre-emption. This is a settled law; reference. if at all necessary, may be made to the decision of the Supreme Court of Pakistan in the case of Begum Asia Rahman, 26 D.L.R, (S.C ) 58, and the decision of this Court in the case of Mofizuddin Patwary; 33 D.L.R. (AD) 305. But the question is whether the alleged separation of Plot No. 108 from Khatian No. 14 was made in conformity with law and to determine this question to what extent a civil court can go into the matter in a collateral proceeding such as the one at hand. 

 17. It appears that some confusion has crept in during the bearing of this appeal because of using, in a loose sense, the terms "separation" and "amalgamation" of holdings. These are quite distinct things each having specific meaning and implication; and as such, these terms should be understood in their proper perspective. For this purpose section 116 and 117(a), 117(c) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, which are relevant in this case, are quoted below: 

 "116. Where various parcels of land are held by one tenant within one village, and such parcels of land or some of them are the subjects to separate tenancies such parcels of land shall under the orders of the Revenue Officer, be amalgamated into one tenancy." 

 (c) for the purpose of subdivision of a joint tenancy for distribution of rent thereof, on an application made to him by one or more co-sharer tenants, direct, by order in writing, such subdivision of a joint tenancy amongst the co-sharer tenants and distribution of rent thereof, including arrears of rent, if any as he may consider fair and equitable: 

 18. It appears clearly that 'amalgamation' means joining of various parcels of lands held by only one tenant so as to constitute one tenancy; and as such it is that tenant's problem alone. No other person, such as his co-sharer, is interested in it and that is why it may be ordered by the Revenue Officer either on his own motion or on an application made to him by the tenant; no notice of the amalgamation is required to be served upon anybody. Sub-division on the other hand, means physical division of a joint-tenancy as well as distribution of the rent thereof among the co-sharer tenants. Sub-division can be made by the Revenue Officer only on an "application made to him by one or" more co-sharer tenants". It shall not be ordered by the Revenue Officer "on his own motion". Secondly, notice of the sub-division shall be served upon all other co-sharers. Non-fulfillment either of these two requirements shall render the order of sub-division void. The term 'separation' is not a legal term like "amalgamation" or "sub-division"; it is not used in section 116 or 117, but nevertheless it denotes in general sense, separation of a share from a joint tenancy and as such 'separation' necessarily means subdivision of a joint tenancy and falls under, and is governed by clause (c) of section 117 Effect of separation of a share from the joint holding falls upon all co-sharers who, after separation, cease to be co-sharers of the original holding. A co-sharer after getting his share separated may get his portion constituted into a new tenancy or he may tag this share with his other land, if any, and if he does so, his case may be referred to as a case of 'separation and ‘amalgamation' for the sake of convenience though the two terms are quite different. His former co-sharers are not interested in such amalgamation. But whether amalgamation or not, for separation of a share from a joint tenancy the two mandatory provisions of clause (c) of section 117 must be first complied with. These provisions cannot be avoided or bypassed by saying that it is not a case of subdivision but it is 'separation and amalgamation'. An undivided share in a joint tenancy cannot be amalgamated with other independent holdings of a co-sharer without first getting his undivided share separated from the joint tenancy. This procedure shall apply even if he has applied for both in the same application. 'Amalgamation' cannot precede 'separation' as cart cannot be put before horse. It is the very case of the appellant that the respondent ceased to be a co-sharer in Khatian 14 from 24 April 1973 when plot 108 was" taken out and constituted into a new tenancy along with his other lands. If the original tenancy was not subdivided how the respondent ceased to be a co-sharer as the appellant claims? Revenue Officer's order shows that the original jama was also divided, out of Tk. 4.45 respondents jama was re-fixed at Tk. 2 55 and that of Percival at Tk. 1.90, which thereafter was added to the jama of the other holdings making his total jam a at Tk. 18.60 for the newly created separate tenancy under Khatian No. 18. This is subdivision pure and simple of the original holding under Khatian No.14. Again, whether a case attracts clause (c) depends upon its nature and implication and not upon how it has been described or designated by the Revenue Officer, The Revenue Officer took this case as 'separation and amalgamation'; but separation as shown above resulted necessarily in subdivision of the old tenancy. 'Separation' is synonymous with 'subdivision' under clause (c) of section 117 The argument that the original holding was not subdivided but was separated and amalgamated is self-defeating and self-contradictory. 

 20. 00 24 April 1973 the Circle Officer (Revenue) passed the final order on receipt of the Tahshilder's report allowing 'separation and amalgamation on the basis of his (Percival's' petition' The trial Court treated the carbon copy of the Certificate Debtor's objection petition as an application for separation of his share in the joint tenancy; but the lower Appellate Court and the High Court Division held that the unsigned carbon copy of an objection petition denying liability in a certificate proceeding under the Public Demands Recovery Act can, under no circumstances. be treated as an application for subdivision or separation of a joint tenancy under the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. In that objection petition, the Certificate debtor did not pray for 'separation or amalgamation' but expressed his readiness to pay the proportionate rent; the objection was filed in 1969 by Percival but he died in August 1971. This objection petition could not have been treated as an application for separation of his share in the joint holding two years after his death. Even if it is taken that Percival while filing the objection petition also intended the petition to be an application for separation of his share in his joint tenancies it abated on his death in 1971 whereupon his legal, representatives were not substituted. In the Certificate proceedings however his legal representatives were brought on record. From the proposal submitted by the Dealing Assistant and the order of the Revenue Officer starting the proceeding for separation and amalgamation, it is crystal clear that the Revenue Officer, whatever might have prompted him, had initiated the matter on his own motion. Had it been the case of mere amalgamation under clause (a) it would have been perfectly lawful. But this being a case of separation first, it comes well within the mischief of clause (c), and the 'separation' not having been made on an application it is void. 

 21. As to the contention about non service of notice-another mandatory provision for separation of the share-it is only the order-sheet of the Mutation case, which shows "notice duly served" Khandker Mahbubuddio Ahmed con- tends that the Record does not contain the. Service Return nor the name and address of Percival's co-sharer were stated in the carbon copy petition nor in any other document or paper of the Record and the Firisti of documents forming the record does not show any paper missing either. In these circumstances, the learned Counsel contends that prima facie this mandatory provision was not complied with by serving notice upon the respondent, The learned Counsel has in this connection relied upon a decision of this Court in the case Abdur Rouf Vs. Amuda Khatun, 33 D.L. R. (A D) 323, wherein if was held that the splitting,up of a joint tenancy effected behind the bat of a co-sharer was void. Mr. Harnidul Huq Chowdhury however, contends that the entry in the order-sheet of the Mutation Case made in usual course of official business is sufficient proof of prima facie service of notice and that in the proceeding for pre-emption the Court is not competent to go further into the matter to ascertain whether the notice the actually served in support of this contention the learned Counsel has referred to another decision of this Court in the case of Md. Jabed Ali Vs. Rakhal Chandra Mondal 33 D.L.R. (A.D.) 309. The purport of that decision is that when an order is passed by a competent Revenue Officer under section 117 of the Act and the order is inconformity with the statutory requirements and the order has been given effect to by the co-sharer tenants of the holding the holding stands separated under law and.................the civil court is not competent to ignore the order on the ground of finding some irregularity in the same as a court of appeal while dealing with the application under section 96 of the Act for pre-emption", I do not find any conflict between these two decisions. The questions raised there related to prima facie compliance of mandatory provisions as to splitting up of a joint tenancy by a competent Revenue Officer and the scope of enquiry in a collateral proceeding. In one case the order for splitting up was found prima facie valid and in the other the order was not so found. These cases were decided on their respective facts and circumstances. In the instant case apart from the question of compliance with the two statutory requirements, there is the question of giving effect to the order for splitting up of joint jam a of Khatian No.14. Though Plot No. 108 was separated and constituted into a new tenancy with effect from 24 April 1973 as alleged by the appellant, the record or right was not amended accordingly until two years after the filing of this pre-emption case. Mr. Hamidul Huq Chowdbury relies upon Ext. R which is purportedly the amended Khatian No. 14 showing the splitting up of the joint tenancy between Percival and the respondent by an order of the Revenue Officer dated "28-1-67". But it also shows that this splitting up of the original jama was made on the basis of the Mutation Case. No. 89 of 1972-73. How the amendment was made six years before the filing of the Mutation Case its basis? Obviously, Ext. R bas been created for the purpose of this instant case and as such is not reliable. As to its rent it continued to be paid at the old rate of Tk. 4.45 till 1978. Tile trial Court is of course right in its observation that mere non-payment of rent at the new rate will not affect the splitting up; but this omission is a factor which must be considered when the question is whether the splitting up order was given effect to as against the consistent claim of the respondent that everything was done behind his knowledge in the Dame of a dead co-sharer. Facts of this case attract Abdur Rouf Vs. Amuda Khatunand not "Jabed Ali Vs. Rakhal Chandra Mondal:" The order of Revenue Officer splitting up a joint-tenancy whichever way it may be designated if it serves the old relationship of its co-sharers and thereby destroys a co-sharer's statutory right of pre-emption, must be examined by the Court in a pre- emption proceeding in order to be satisfied that prima facie the order was passed in accordance with law, that is to say the mandatory provisions of section 117(c) were complied with on the face of the record. The scope of this examination cannot be so limited as to ask the Court to keep its eyes closed and to accept without hesitation whatever order is placed before it simply because the order was passed by a competent Revenue Officer. Khandker Mahbubuddin Ahmed has submitted that the scope of enquiry in a case for pre-emption is wide enough to include the question of benami transaction in certain cases placing his reliance upon the case of Balai Chandra Mondal Vs. Nibaran Chandra Das 51 C.W.N. 644. In that case two long lines of cases, one line reo presenting the view that question of benami was outside the scope of s. 26F of the Bengal Tenancy Act and the other line representing the contrary view were elaborately discussed and considered and it was held that the question of benami transaction fell within the scope of s. 26F only in two classes of cases. In one class, the transfer is made to a co-sharer tenant in the benami of a stranger, and in the other class no transfer at all takes place but a show of transfer is made as in the case of plaintiff Nibaran. The suit was decreed and the order of pre-emption was declared void. 

 22. In the instant case it has been argued, the aggrieved co-sharer got proper remedy against the Revenue Officer's order by appeal. But his case is that the whole matter was manipulated after Percival's death and behind his knowledge and as such he got no opportunity to seek remedy by appeal. Be that as it may, on perusal of the records of the Miscellaneous case I find no difficulty to bold that the proceeding for separation of Plot No. 108 from Kbatian No. 14 was void ab initio as it was taken suo motu by the Revenue Officer and behind the co-sharer's knowledge and consequently the joint tenancy was Dot divided but it still continues and this being the position the pre-emption is a co-sharer in the holding having right to pre-emption. I find nothing to interfere with the order of the High Court Division which rightly confirmed that of the lower appellate Court. I would therefore dismiss the appeal' with costs.
